questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Berkeley is known for having one of the best economics departments in the world. Acces to courses taught by world-renowned professors drew me to Berkeley.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Would recommend anyone going on exchange.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: At first it's a little confusing getting to know all the different Berkeley websites and such, but you'll get a hang of it.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Unfortunately orientation was online - even though courses were taught in-person just a couple weeks later - which was rather boring. But the information that was conveyed was fine. There's a lot of focus on alcohol and drug abuse and mental health, and they tell you how to tackle that regarding to yourself or friends.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think i was unlucky with my orientation leaders.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Berkeley had a few tips to finding housing, and they also recommend I-house and the Co-op system. You have to apply to both places, and make sure to do it early. For the Co-ops you get priority for being an international student. The co-ops are definitely the cheapest housing option. 

I lived with 36 Americans at Ridge House, which was great. I think the people at I-house had a great time too, although that's mostly other international students. 

I also joined facebook groups for housing. I was lucky to be offered the co-op just a couple weeks before leaving for Berkeley, but otherwise I would have flown to Berkeley and stayed at a hotel for a while, while checking out renting options. 

A lot of people also stay at private share-houses, which are similar to the co-ops but much more expensive. 

One tip is to stay as close to campus as possible - you don't want to have to walk too far (especially at night), since social life is centered around campus and just off campus on the south side mostly.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Most co-ops are on North side of campus, while most other student housing is on South side.
I enjoyed living on North side - there's a few cafes and restaurants, but things close early. On south side is where the bars are, and this is were you go out. However the walk to South side from North is short (maybe 10-15 min), and I was never scared to walk through campus at night. 

Only freshmen live on-campus. You don't want that.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I can really recommend Ridge House, it has a lot of common space compared to other co-ops I saw and it has a beautiful garden and terrace where we would hang out. Ridge has 37 people and was super social. Everybody knows everybody well and there was always someone hanging out in the kitchen at home. The house would always each together at 7 pm, and there would always still be people hanging out in the dining room if you were home late for dinner. 

The co-ops are great because there is always food (which is stocked by the food manager) and you can take whatever you want whenever. I know in I-house you can't cook for yourself, and food is only available at certain hours of the day. 

In the co-ops the rent is cheap and includes food, but then you have to do 5 hours of workshift every week. I did kitchen cleaning, garden, food delivery put-away. It was fine.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Was a little confusing at first, but you'll figure it out. They have guides online. 
Even though we were told we could only expect to take 2 economics courses, mostly everybody took all economics courses. Don't know why they tell you that..

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I picked out the courses I was interested in from the course website. Remember to check how full they are, and whether you can expect to get a spot by the time your course registration opens. I think seniors and athletes get to pick courses first, so popular courses can be filled up before you even get to register. Then you go to calcentral (their kunet) and register in the middle of the night when it opens.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They had guides online

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Some classes I was originally interested in were already full by the time my registration opened. But there are so many great courses to choose from, so finding replacements wasn't difficult.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Wake up in the middle of the night for it - courses fill up fast! Have the courses ready in your shopping cart, so that you only have to click 1 button when registration opens.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some courses were easier than what I was used to from UCPH but others more difficult.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was more relaxed than at UCPH. Classes were generally smaller, and there was more interaction with professors.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
143 - Econometrics: Advanced Methods and Applications (with Bryan Graham) 
134 - MACROECONOMIC POLICY FROM THE GREAT DEPRESSION TO TODAY 
191 - Topics in Economic Research (seminar with David Card) 
171 - Development Economics (with Ben Faber)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
All of them really. 143 was amazing! One of the best courses I've taken in my lives. 
134 was not very technical, but extremely interesting. 
171 was amazing as well. It introduced a wide variety of topics in development economics. 
191 was just a seminar, but they had very interesting guest lecturers come in and talk about their research.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Berkeley has clubs, but they're a little difficult to figure out as an international student.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to sporting events and experience the schools spirit.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to SF, Las Vegas, Sonoma or Napa, Monterrey, Carmel by the Sea, Oakland, Yosemite. There's lots to see around the Bay Area.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Maybe drug use - seems more common in the US than what I'm used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are generally more outgoing and willing to help each other than I typically feel like Danish people are.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Go on lots of trips and explore California.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The courses were awesome. The opportunities for taking trips was great.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Midterm season can be overwhelming, but hang in there.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
